source_text: Βασιλείδης δὲ ἐν τῷ εἰκοστῷ τρίτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸ μαρτύριον κολαζομένων αὐταῖς λέξεσι τάδε φησί· φημὶ γάρ τοι, ὁπόσοι ὑποπίπτουσι ταῖς λεγομέναις θλίψεσιν, ἤτοι ἡμαρτηκότες ἐν ἄλλοις λανθάνοντες πταίσμασιν εἰς τοῦτο ἄγονται τὸ ἀγαθόν, χρηστότητι τοῦ περιάγοντος ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλλων ὄντως ἐγκαλούμενοι, ἵνα μὴ ὡς κατάδικοι ἐπὶ κακοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις πάθωσι, μηδὲ λοιδορούμενοι ὡς ὁ μοιχὸς ἢ ὁ φονεύς, ἀλλ’ ὅτι Χριστιανοὶ † πεφυκότες, ὅπερ αὐτοὺς παρηγορήσει μηδὲ πάσχειν δοκεῖν· κἂν μὴ ἡμαρτηκὼς δ’ ὅλως τις ἐπὶ τὸ παθεῖν γένηται, σπάνιον μέν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ οὗτος κατ’ ἐπιβουλὴν δυνάμεώς τι πείσεται, ἀλλὰ πείσεται ὡς ἔπασχε καὶ τὸ νήπιον τὸ δοκοῦν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκέναι. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς πάλιν ἐπιφέρει· ὡς οὖν τὸ νήπιον οὐ προημαρτηκὸς ἢ ἐνεργῶς μὲν οὐχ ἡμαρτηκὸς οὐδέν, ἐν ἑαυτῷ τῷ δὲ τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαι ἔχον, ἐπὰν ὑποβληθῇ τῷ παθεῖν, εὐεργετεῖται τε, πολλὰ κερδαῖνον δύσκολα, οὑτωσὶ δὴ κἂν τέλειος μηδὲν ἡμαρτηκὼς ἔργῳ τύχῃ, δέ, ἃν πάθῃ, τοῦτο ἔπαθεν ἐμφερῶς τῷ νηπίῳ· ἔχων μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἁμαρτητικόν, ἀφορμὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι μὴ λαβὼν οὐχ ἡμάρτανεν. ὥστ’ οὐκ αὐτῷ τὸ μὴ ἁμαρτῆσαι λογιστέον. ὡς γὰρ ὁ μοιχεῦσαι θέλων μοιχός ἐστι, κἂν τοῦ μοιχεῦσαι μὴ ἐπιτύχῃ, καὶ ὁ ποιῆσαι φόνον θέλων ἀνδροφόνος ἐστί, κἂν μὴ δύνηται φονεῦσαι, οὑτωσὶ δὴ καὶ τὸν ἀναμάρτητον ὃν λέγω ἐὰν ἴδω πάσχοντα, κἂν μηδὲν ᾖ κακὸν πεπραχώς, κακὸν ἐρῶ τῷ θέλειν ἁμαρτάνειν. πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ. εἶθ’ ὑποβὰς καὶ περὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἄντικρυς ὡς περὶ ἀνθρώπου λέγει· ἐὰν μέντοι παραλιπὼν τούτους ἅπαντας τοὺς λόγους ἔλθῃς ἐπὶ τὸ δυσωπεῖν με διὰ προσώπων τινῶν, εἰ τύχοι, λέγων, ὁ δεῖνα οὖν ἥμαρτεν, ἔπαθεν γὰρ ὁ δεῖνα, ἐὰν μὲν ἐπιτρέπῃς, ἐρῶ, οὐχ ἥμαρτεν μέν, ὅμοιος δὲ ἦν τῷ πάσχοντι νηπίῳ· εἰ μέντοι σφοδρότερον ἐκβιάσαιο τὸν λόγον, ἐρῶ, ἄνθρωπον ὅντιν’ ἂν ὀνομάσῃς ἄνθρωπον εἶναι, δίκαιον δὲ τὸν θεόν. καθαρὸς γὰρ οὐδείς, ὥσπερ εἶπέ τις, ἀπὸ ῥύπου. ἀλλὰ τῷ Βασιλείδῃ ἡ ὑπόθεσις προαμαρτήσασάν φησι τὴν ψυχὴν ἐν ἑτέρῳ βίῳ τὴν κόλασιν ὑπομένειν ἐνταῦθα, τὴν μὲν ἐκλεκτὴν ἐπιτίμως διὰ μαρτυρίου, τὴν ἄλλην δὲ καθαιρομένην οἰκείᾳ κολάσει.
pass_a_gloss: Basilides, in the twenty-third of the Exegetical works, concerning those punished according to the testimony, says the following: For I say that as many as fall into the so-called afflictions, either having sinned in other respects and escaping notice, are led to this good thing by the kindness of the One who leads them, so that they may not suffer as condemned for acknowledged evils, nor be reviled as an adulterer or a murderer, but because they have been born as Christians, which will comfort them and make them seem not to suffer. And even if someone has not sinned at all and is led to suffer, this is rare, but he will not suffer by the force of power, but will suffer as the innocent child suffers. Then, proceeding further, he says: Just as the child is not a pre-sinner, nor has sinned in action, but has the potential to sin within itself, and when it is subjected to suffering, it is benefited and gains much, even in difficulties, so also if a perfect person, who has not sinned in deed, happens to suffer, he suffers similarly to the child, having the potential to sin within himself, but not having taken the opportunity to sin, he has not sinned. Therefore, it should not be reckoned to him that he has not sinned. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not succeed in committing adultery, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer, even if he is not able to kill, so also the one I call sinless, if I see him suffering, even if he has not done anything evil, I will say that he is evil in his willingness to sin. I will say that all things are more than evil, I will say that forethought is evil. Then, proceeding further and speaking about the Lord as if about a man, he says: But if, leaving all these words aside, you come to calumniating me through certain persons, saying, for example, that so-and-so sinned and suffered, if you permit, I will say that he did not sin, but was similar to the suffering child. But if you force the argument more strongly, I will say that whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure, as someone has said, from filth. But Basilides' hypothesis says that the soul, having pre-sinned in another life, endures punishment here, the elect suffering through martyrdom, and the others being purified by their own punishment.
pass_b_english: In the twenty-third book of his Exegetical works, Basilides offers the following observations about those punished for their testimony. He declares that all who fall into these so-called afflictions fall into two groups. Some have sinned in other matters and escaped notice; the kindness of the One who governs all things leads them to this good outcome so that they will not suffer as condemned men for acknowledged evils, nor be reviled as an adulterer or a murderer, but because they have been born Christians. That identity will comfort them and make it seem as though they do not suffer at all. Even if someone has not sinned at all and is brought to suffering, such a case is rare, but neither will that person suffer by the force of hostile power; rather, he will suffer as the innocent child suffers.

Pursuing the argument further, Basilides explains: just as the child has not sinned beforehand nor actively sinned in deed, yet possesses within itself the capacity to sin, and when subjected to suffering is benefited and gains much even amid hardship, so also a perfect person who has not sinned in deed, if he happens to suffer, suffers in the same way as the child. He has the potential for sin within himself, but because he did not receive the opportunity to sin, he did not commit sin. Therefore, it must not be credited to him that he has not sinned. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer even if he does not succeed, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer even if he is unable to kill, so too the one I call sinless, if I see him suffering, even if he has done nothing evil, I will declare him evil in his willingness to sin. I will say that all things are evil rather than say that divine providence is evil.

Then, advancing the argument still further and speaking of the Lord as if He were a mere man, Basilides says: but if you set aside all these arguments and come to calumniate me through certain persons, saying, for example, that so-and-so sinned and therefore suffered, if you permit, I will answer that he did not sin but was like the suffering child. However, if you press the argument more forcefully, I will say that whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure from filth, as someone has said. Yet Basilides' hypothesis maintains that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, endures punishment here: the elect through martyrdom, and the rest being purified by their own punishment.

review.notes: Pass A fails to translate the clause 'πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ' correctly. Pass A translates it as 'I will say that all things are more than evil, I will say that forethought is evil', whereas the Greek 'πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ' means 'For I will say all [things] are evil rather than say that providence is evil'. Pass A's rendering 'more than evil' is a mistranslation of 'μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν' (rather than evil). Pass B correctly identifies 'divine providence' for 'τὸ προνοοῦν', but Pass A's failure to preserve the sense of the comparison makes the translation inaccurate.
reasons: Pass A mistranslates 'πάντ’ ἐρῶ γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ κακὸν τὸ προνοοῦν ἐρῶ' as 'I will say that all things are more than evil, I will say that forethought is evil', which reverses/distorts the comparative sense of 'rather than' (μᾶλλον ἢ) and the object of the comparison.

review.notes: The Greek text is correctly identified as Basilides' Exegetical works, and the translation accurately reflects the content. The passage is complete, and all key concepts such as sin, suffering, and the role of the soul are preserved. Scripture citations are not present in this excerpt, so no issues there. The title 'Martyrdom and Sin' appropriately captures the theme. No OCR damage or uncertainties are noted.
